cover_headline: A Firing Squad and a Livestream

cover_text.headline: A Firing Squad and a Livestream
cover_text.text:
The U.S. Army scheduled the execution of Nidal Malik Hasan for December 3, setting the date for the Fort Hood mass shooter to die by firing squad at the Texas military installation where he killed 13 people in 2009.

Hasan, an Army major and psychiatrist, opened fire inside Fort Hood’s Soldier Readiness Processing Center on November 5, 2009. Witnesses testified he shouted "Allahu akbar" before firing a laser-sighted handgun, killing 13 individuals and attempting to kill another 32. He later told the court he had switched sides, acting to prevent American troops from deploying to Afghanistan. A military panel unanimously convicted Hasan on August 28, 2013, of 13 counts of premeditated murder and 32 counts of attempted premeditated murder. The panel sentenced him to death, dismissal from the Army, and forfeiture of his pay and allowances. Hasan exhausted the direct military appellate process, with the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Armed Forces affirming his case in March 2024. The Supreme Court denied his petition for review on March 31, 2025.

Republican Florida Governor Ron DeSantis called it "appropriate punishment for a terrorist!" Republican Senator Ted Cruz of Texas approved the decision, stating Hasan "deserves to be executed for his crimes."

Two days later, on October 8, the Pentagon confirmed plans to livestream the execution. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth stated, "We'll make sure that people are able to watch it, that it's public." President Trump remarked that Hasan "deserves it for killing and wounding many people." The UN’s High Commissioner for Human Rights condemned the livestreaming, stating it was "tantamount to a public execution" and would "breach the absolute prohibition of torture." Archbishop Paul Coakley, president of the US Conference of Catholic Bishops, called it "a barbaric promotion of a culture of death and must be reconsidered." Alonzo Lunsford, a Fort Hood survivor shot seven times, supported the execution but expressed reservations about uncensored public viewing, stating, "To show the whole thing without it being censored for the general public, for me personally, I don’t agree with that." Lunsford plans to attend the execution in person.

The following day, October 9, a Pentagon official reiterated that Hasan's execution would be livestreamed. Kristopher Craig, brother of Army Pfc. Michael Pearson, a soldier killed in the 2009 shooting, began drafting a letter to President Trump and Defense Secretary Hegseth, urging them to reconsider the livestream plan. Lawmakers from both political parties voiced opposition. Senator Thom Tillis, a Republican, called the plan "beyond disgusting." Senator Lisa Murkowski, also a Republican, urged the Pentagon to reverse its decision, stating, "I would expect this from terrorists and dictators, but not here in" the US. Vice President JD Vance cast doubt on whether the execution would actually be livestreamed, stating he "would not watch if it is." Austin Sarat, a professor at Amherst College, stated that livestreaming the execution "will turn that brutality into a spectacle of cruelty and will not educate."

President Trump, however, stated he "will ultimately make the decision" on whether to proceed with the livestream. Concerns emerged that livestreaming the execution could turn Hasan into a martyr for his cause. Alonzo Lunsford, the survivor shot seven times, reiterated his plan to attend the execution to "lock eyes with the shooter," but remained uncomfortable with the public livestream, suggesting it should be restricted to survivors and victims' families. The United Nations called the plan "abhorrent," and Amnesty International described it as "barbaric and deeply shocking." Pentagon officials expressed internal concerns about the psychological impact on soldiers tasked with carrying out the execution.

cover_text.headline: Political Transitions and Market Scrutiny
cover_text.text:
Her new role is set to begin on November 1, with plans for her to provide commentary across the Fox News lineup and its media platforms. Fox News Media CEO Suzanne Scott stated that Leavitt's "firsthand experience in the White House and on the presidential campaign trail gives her a distinct understanding of today's political landscape." She expressed looking forward to bringing her "unique perspective, energy, and candor" to Fox's viewers.

Leavitt had stepped down from the Trump administration at the end of August. President Donald Trump described her as "one of his most trusted aides" and stated she would "remain a top outside advisor and an influential voice within the Republican Party." Fox News agreed to build a studio in Leavitt's New Hampshire home to facilitate her new role. Her professional career began as a deputy press secretary during President Trump’s first administration, after interning at local news organizations as a student. She later ran for Congress and worked for Trump’s 2024 campaign, marking her first direct engagement with a major news organization in her professional career.

President Donald Trump appointed Katie Zacharia as the new White House Press Secretary. Trump announced the appointment on Truth Social, praising Zacharia's "unblemished record of support" and calling her a "loyal and brilliant supporter." Zacharia, a conservative commentator and lawyer, responded on X, calling the appointment "the honor of a lifetime."

Zacharia's professional background includes serving as a senior communications adviser for Trump Media & Technology Group since June, and as a spokesperson for the Department of Homeland Security. She also held the position of general counsel at Fix California, a conservative activist group. Her appointment prompted an investigation by the prediction market Kalshi into suspicious betting activity. Three traders placed wagers on Zacharia's chances on the Kalshi platform shortly before news outlets began announcing her appointment. Zacharia had been widely seen as having only a 1 percent chance of becoming press secretary. These small but well-timed wagers offered an opportunity for bettors to make thousands of dollars. One $19 bet was slated to pay out $1,896, while bets of $74 and $80 were expected to pay out $3,689 and $4,023 respectively. This activity follows a prior incident where White House teleprompter operator Gabriel Perez was fired for collecting over $100,000 on bets about presidential speeches. Zacharia herself has a history of promoting claims, including an argument made on X in November 2025, linking the abortion pill mifepristone to Nazi concentration camps.

opinion_text:
The U.S. Army scheduled the execution of Nidal Malik Hasan for December 3, setting the date for the Fort Hood mass shooter to die by firing squad. Hasan, an Army major and psychiatrist, killed 13 people and attempted to kill 32 others in 2009, shouting "Allahu akbar." A military panel convicted him in 2013, sentencing him to death. His appeals exhausted, the Supreme Court denied review in 2025. The state, through its military arm, is exercising its ultimate authority, bringing a final, irreversible consequence after a long, deliberate process.

Her new role begins November 1. She stepped down from the administration at the end of August, citing a desire to spend time with her young children. Fox News agreed to build a studio in her New Hampshire home. This transition illustrates a rapid monetization of political access, where proximity to power translates into immediate private gain.

This week, we observe a pattern: the swiftness of both ultimate consequence and immediate reward, dictated by an individual's relationship to concentrated power. Whether it is the state's final judgment or the media's lucrative embrace, the mechanisms of accountability and advancement are increasingly defined by this proximity. This blurs the lines between public service and private interest, eroding the foundational integrity of our institutions.

Some might argue that Leavitt's move is a natural progression in a free market, a reward for talent and experience. Others might see Hasan's execution as long-overdue justice, a necessary act to uphold the rule of law. We acknowledge these perspectives. However, the speed and nature of these outcomes raise questions about the true cost to the public. When public service becomes a clear stepping stone to private enrichment, the very idea of selfless duty is undermined. When the state's ultimate power is exercised, the solemnity of that act must be beyond reproach, not merely a political approval.

The public, who did not consent to these arrangements, pays the cost in diminished trust. We are left to consider what kind of society is built when the rewards of political access are so immediate and substantial, and when the ultimate power of the state is wielded with such finality. The week's events demonstrate how concentrated power, regardless of intent, shapes the landscape of both justice and opportunity, often at the expense of institutional restraint and public faith.

opinions.headline: The Spectacle of State-Sanctioned Violence
opinions.text:
The Army’s decision to schedule Nidal Hasan’s execution by firing squad on December 3 at Fort Hood, and the subsequent Pentagon plan to livestream this event, transforms a judicial sentence into a public spectacle. This is not justice; it is a performance of state power that risks dehumanizing both the condemned and the viewers. The stated intention, as articulated by Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, is to "show serious consequences for these types of things." However, the proposed livestreaming, condemned by the UN’s High Commissioner for Human Rights as "tantamount to a public execution" and by Archbishop Paul Coakley as a "barbaric promotion of a culture of death," risks turning a solemn act into a cruel exhibition.

Hasan, a former Army psychiatrist, killed 13 people and wounded 32 in 2009. His conviction and death sentence are established facts. Yet, the method of execution and its public broadcast raise profound ethical questions. The plan to use a firing squad follows a series of botched lethal injections, a practical concern that should not overshadow the moral implications of state-sanctioned killing. The UN’s condemnation highlights the international standard against torture and cruel punishment, a standard that livestreaming a death sentence arguably violates.

The desire to make the execution public, to "show serious consequences," is understandable in the face of such horrific violence. Alonzo Lunsford, a survivor shot seven times, plans to attend, seeking to "lock eyes with Hasan." His sentiment, however, is tempered by reservations about "uncensored public viewing," stating, "To show the whole thing without it being censored for the general public, for me personally, I don’t agree with that." This reflects a tension between the desire for closure and the potential for gratuitous cruelty. The argument that this will serve as a deterrent or a clear message of consequence is undermined by the very real concern that it could instead turn Hasan into a martyr for his cause, as some reports suggest.

The decision to livestream the execution has drawn bipartisan criticism. Republican Senator Thom Tillis called the plan "beyond disgusting," and Republican Senator Lisa Murkowski urged the Pentagon to reverse its decision, stating, "I would expect this from terrorists and dictators, but not here in" the US. This widespread condemnation from across the political spectrum and from religious leaders, including Pope Leo XIV, suggests a fundamental disconnect between the Pentagon's plan and broader societal values.

The ultimate decision rests with President Donald Trump, who has indicated he will make the final call on the livestream. Given the ethical concerns raised by survivors, lawmakers, and international bodies, the President should reconsider this plan. Instead of a public broadcast, the focus should remain on the solemnity of the sentence and the memory of the victims, without turning their tragedy into a spectacle. The Pentagon should abandon the livestreaming plan and proceed with the execution in a manner that respects human dignity, even in the face of profound evil.

opinions.headline: Justice Delayed, Justice Denied
opinions.text:
The Army’s decision to schedule Nidal Hasan’s execution by firing squad on December 3 at Fort Hood, Texas, brings a measure of closure to a brutal chapter. Hasan, an Army psychiatrist, unleashed a torrent of bullets on November 5, 2009, killing 13 and wounding 32. His stated motive: to prevent American troops from deploying to Afghanistan and to act in defense of Muslims. A military panel found him guilty of 13 counts of premeditated murder and 32 counts of attempted premeditated murder, sentencing him to death. This sentence, affirmed by the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Armed Forces in March 2024 and left standing by the Supreme Court’s denial of review on March 31, 2025, is now set to be carried out.

President Donald Trump approved the execution, following Secretary of War Pete Hegseth’s recommendation. This marks the first military execution since 1961, and the first by firing squad since 1945. The choice of firing squad itself is a return to a method that predates the modern era of state-sanctioned killing, a stark contrast to the often-troubled lethal injections that have plagued recent executions.

The plan to livestream this execution, however, has drawn considerable opposition. Defense Secretary Hegseth stated the intention is to show "serious consequences for these types of things." Yet, critics, including Archbishop Paul Coakley, president of the U.S. Conference of Catholic Bishops, have called it a "barbaric promotion of a culture of death." The UN’s High Commissioner for Human Rights condemned it as "tantamount to a public execution." Even Alonzo Lunsford, a survivor of Hasan’s attack who plans to attend, expressed reservations about uncensored public viewing, stating, "To show the whole thing without it being censored for the general public, for me personally, I don’t agree with that."

While the desire to make the consequences of Hasan's actions clear is understandable, turning his execution into a spectacle risks demeaning the gravity of the event and the suffering of the victims. The purpose of justice is not entertainment, nor is it to create martyrs. The precedent of military executions, while established, has been dormant for decades. The decision to revive it, coupled with the controversial plan for a livestream, demands careful consideration of the message it sends.

The execution should proceed as scheduled, but the livestream should be reconsidered. The victims and their families deserve justice, but the state should not engage in acts that could be perceived as gratuitous or that risk glorifying violence.

opinions.headline: Karoline Leavitt's New Role at Fox News
opinions.text:
Karoline Leavitt, formerly President Donald Trump’s press secretary, is joining Fox News as an on-air contributor starting November 1. Her new role will involve providing commentary across the Fox News lineup and its media platforms. Fox News Media CEO Suzanne Scott stated that Leavitt's "firsthand experience in the White House and on the presidential campaign trail gives her a distinct understanding of today's political landscape." Leavitt, 29, expressed her eagerness to bring her "unique perspective, energy, and candor" to the network's viewers.

Following her departure from the administration, Leavitt rejoined the Trump-affiliated super PAC MAGA Inc. and spoke at the Republican Midterm Convention in early September. This move to Fox News marks her first direct professional engagement with a major news organization. Fox News has agreed to build a studio in Leavitt's New Hampshire home for her new role.

The appointment follows President Trump’s selection of Katie Zacharia as his new White House Press Secretary on Friday, replacing Leavitt. Zacharia, a conservative commentator and lawyer, previously served as a senior communications adviser for Trump Media & Technology Group. The news of Zacharia's appointment has drawn attention due to suspicious betting activity on prediction market Kalshi, where traders placed bets on her selection shortly before it was announced. Zacharia was widely considered to have a low chance of securing the position.

While Leavitt's transition to a media role is a common path for former political appointees, some reporting has highlighted a perceived inconsistency. This perspective suggests a potential hypocrisy in her new work-from-home setup.

Leavitt's supporters, including President Trump, view her as a trusted aide and an influential voice within the Republican Party. Her new role at Fox News will allow her to continue engaging with political discourse. Given the established practice of former administration officials joining media outlets, Leavitt's move is not unexpected. Her ability to articulate her perspective will be tested by the network's audience and the broader political commentary landscape.

opinions.headline: The White House Defends Trump Remark on Iran Taking Out Los Angeles, San Diego
opinions.text:
President Donald Trump’s suggestion at a Nebraska rally that Iran could “take out Los Angeles, let ‘em take out San Diego” and that this was “a very small price to pay” has drawn predictable outrage from California leaders. Governor Gavin Newsom called the remarks “deranged and dangerous,” while Los Angeles Mayor Karen Bass stated they were threats and an attempt to encourage attacks. San Diego Mayor Todd Gloria declared the city “not collateral damage.” These reactions are understandable; no American city should be treated as expendable.

The White House, however, has defended Trump’s comments, with Communications Director Steven Cheung stating on X that the media’s reaction was “not rooted in reality.” Cheung clarified that Trump was “clearly stating US cities would have been threatened if a nuclear Iran hadn't been stopped.” This interpretation suggests Trump was illustrating a hypothetical consequence of a nuclear Iran, not advocating for such an attack. CNN fact-checker Daniel Dale also provided a fuller transcript, suggesting Trump was taken out of context and was saying the opposite of what critics claimed. Trump himself later attempted to clarify at a rally in San Antonio, Texas, reiterating that Iran could hit the cities on the way but assuring the crowd such an attack would not occur.

While the immediate shock value of Trump’s phrasing is undeniable, the White House’s defense, supported by a closer look at the transcript, points to a misinterpretation. Trump was discussing the economic costs of war, including higher prices, and framed the potential threat to American cities as a “small price to pay” for global and national safety, implying that preventing a nuclear Iran was the paramount concern. The audience’s cheers after his comments, noted in some reports, suggest a segment of the crowd understood his remarks within this context of deterrence.

Mayor Bass indicated she might call on Congress to investigate Trump's comments. Given the potential for such statements to be misconstrued or weaponized, a more formal review of the full context and intent behind Trump's remarks could be beneficial.

opinions.headline: Diesel Deal Fuels Controversy
opinions.text:
This agreement, brokered between President Donald Trump and Russian President Vladimir Putin, comes with a temporary waiver of U.S. sanctions on Russia's energy sector. President Trump stated the deal's aim is to lower diesel prices for American consumers, farmers, ranchers, and truckers, particularly ahead of the midterm elections.

However, the market signals here are mixed, and the unintended consequences could be substantial. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy sharply criticized the deal, calling it a "birthday gift" to Putin that would finance Russia's war. EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas and Germany indicated they would continue to push for sanctions. A U.S. official suggested the deal was a response to Ukrainian President Zelenskyy ignoring U.S. requests to stop strikes on Russian oil refineries, which had reportedly caused a crisis for Putin.

While President Trump frames the agreement as a pragmatic move to address domestic energy costs, the market’s reaction and the geopolitical implications warrant scrutiny. The Straits Times notes an analysis suggesting the deal is "unlikely to cut prices" due to small volumes and global market pricing. This raises questions about the actual economic benefit for American consumers versus the potential for emboldening Russia.

The timing is also critical. This raises concerns about whether the deal inadvertently provides Russia with the resources to continue its military actions.

This stance, coupled with the diesel deal, has drawn objections from some Republican lawmakers.

The core economic incentive for President Trump appears to be lowering domestic fuel costs. Yet, the market signal sent to Russia, and the potential for that nation to leverage any perceived easing of pressure, is a counterpoint. The decision to waive sanctions, even temporarily, risks undermining broader efforts to isolate Russia economically.

Moving forward, the actual impact on diesel prices will be the ultimate market test. If prices do not fall substantially, the justification for the sanctions waiver weakens considerably, and the geopolitical risks become more pronounced. The administration should closely monitor global diesel markets and the flow of funds to Russia, prepared to reinstate sanctions if the economic benefits to the U.S. do not materialize or if Russia escalates its aggression.
